Case Number: 25NNCV06429    Hearing Date: July 31, 2026    Dept: A

 

TENTATIVE RULING

JULY 31, 2026

MOTIONS TO COMPEL RESPONSES

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV06429

 

MP:     Defendant Ross Dress for Less, Inc.

RP:      No opposition received

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at [email protected] or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

MOTIONS ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 10, 2026, Ross Dress for Less, Inc. (“Defendant”) filed three motions to compel Esthela Garcia’s (“Plaintiff”) initial responses to: (1) Form Interrogatories (“FROG”), set one; (2) Special Interrogatories (“SROG”), set one; and (3) Request for Production of Documents (“RPD”), set one.  On July 24, 2026, Defendant filed Notice of Non-Receipt of Opposition to the three motions.  (The oppositions were due by July 20, 2026.) The Court is not in receipt of an opposition brief.  The Court notes that, pursuant to C.R.C. Rule 8.54(c), a failure to oppose a motion may be deemed consent to its being granted.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

If a party to whom interrogatories are directed fails to serve a timely response, the propounding party may move for an order compelling response and for a monetary sanction.  (C.C.P. § 2030.290(b).)  The statute contains no time limit for a motion to compel where no responses have been served.  All that need be shown in the moving papers is that a set of interrogatories was properly served on the opposing party, that the time to respond has expired, and that no response of any kind has been served.  (See Leach v. Superior Court (1980) 111 Cal. App. 3d 902, 905-906.) 

 

Where there has been no timely response to a demand to produce documents, the demanding party may seek an order compelling a response.  (C.C.P. § 2031.300(b).)  Failure to timely respond waives all objections, including privilege and work product.  (C.C.P. § 2031.300(a).)  Thus, unless the party to whom the demand was directed obtains relief from waiver, he or she cannot raise objections to the documents demanded. There is no deadline for a motion to compel responses.  Likewise, for failure to respond, the moving party need not attempt to resolve the matter outside court before filing the motion. 

 

ANALYSIS: 

 

A.     Discussion

 

On October 16, 2025, Defendant served on Plaintiff the discovery requests, such that responses were due by November 18, 2025.  On December 11, 2025, defense counsel emailed Plaintiff’s counsel requesting the status of discovery responses.  Plaintiff’s counsel requested and Defendant granted a two-week extension.  On February 13, 2026, Defendant requested responses no later than February 18, 2026.  On February 15, 2026, Plaintiff’s requested a second two-week extension.  On March 16, 2026, Defendant followed-up and Plaintiff’s counsel requested a third two-week extension.  On March 27, 2026, defense counsel left a voicemail for Plaintiff’s counsel regarding the outstanding discovery and Plaintiff’s counsel responded they were having difficulty contacting their client and requested a fourth two-week extension.  As of the filing of the motions, Defendant states that it has not received Plaintiff’s responses. 

 

Defendant’s unopposed motions to compel responses to the FROG, SROG, and RPD are granted pursuant to C.C.P. §§ 2030.290 and 2031.300.  Plaintiff is ordered to provide verified responses to the discovery requests, without objections, within 30 days of this order.

 

B.     Sanctions

 

The Court has discretion to impose a monetary sanction against a party engaging in the misuse of the discovery process, or any attorney advising that conduct. (C.C.P. § 2023.030(a).) Sanctions are only mandatory as against a party who unsuccessfully makes or opposes a motion to compel a response to interrogatories or RPD, unless the Court finds they acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust. (C.C.P. §§ 2030.290(c) & 2031.300(c).) Regardless, it is customary to grant sanctions where a party has filed a motion to compel, and the other party fails to file an opposition. (C.R.C. Rule 3.1348(a).) 

 

Defendant requests $1,915 in sanctions against Plaintiff and her attorney per motion (= [4 hours for the motion + 2 anticipated hours to review the opposition, draft the reply, and attend the hearing at $265/hour] + $60 in filing fees).  The requests are granted in the reasonable amount of $530 in attorney’s fees and $60 in filing fees (or $590) per motion.  The Court finds that this amount is reasonable as these are straightforward, unopposed motions to compel initial responses and are partially duplicative in nature.  Based on the meet and confer efforts, the Court imposes sanctions as against Plaintiff only and not against Plaintiff’s counsel.

 

--- 

 

RULING:

 

In the event the parties submit on this tentative ruling, or a party requests a signed order or the court in its discretion elects to sign a formal order, the following form will be either electronically signed or signed in hard copy and entered into the court’s records. 

 

ORDER 

 

Defendant Ross Dress for Less, Inc.’s Motions to Compel Responses and Motion to Deem the RFAs Admitted came on regularly for hearing on July 31, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows: 

 

THE MOTIONS TO COMPEL PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSES TO FORM INTERROGATORIES, SPECIAL INTERROGATORIES, AND REQUESTS FOR PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENTS ARE GRANTED.  RESPONSES ARE TO BE MADE WITHIN 30 DAYS.

 

Plaintiff IS ordered to pay $1,590 in monetary sanctions to Defendant, by and through counsel, within 30 days of this order.  NO SANCTIONS ARE IMPOSED AGAINST PLAINTIFF’S COUNSEL.

 

DEFENDANT TO PROVIDE NOTICE.

 

IT IS SO ORDERED. 


Case Number: 25NNCV07958    Hearing Date: July 31, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

JULY 31, 2026

MOTION TO COMPEL FURTHER RESPONSES

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV07958

 

MP:     Plaintiffs Tereza Shahbazian and Emil Golanians

RP:      No opposition received

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at [email protected] or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Tereza Shahbazian and Emil Golanians (“Plaintiffs”) allege that on February 26, 2023, they purchased a 2023 Honda CR-V, which was accompanied by express and implied warranties from American Honda Motor Co., Inc. (“Defendant”).  Plaintiffs assert that the vehicle was delivered with serious defects and nonconformities to the warranty, including transmission, suspension, structural, and electrical system defects.  Plaintiffs claim that despite a reasonable number of repair attempts, Defendant was unable to conform the vehicle to applicable warranties. 

 

The Complaint, filed November 7, 2025, alleges causes of action for: (1) Violation of Song-Beverly Act – Breach of Express Warranty; (2) Violation of Song-Beverly Act – Breach of Implied Warranty; and (3) Violation of the Song-Beverly Act, § 1793.2. 

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 24, 2026, Plaintiffs filed a Motion to Compel Defendant’s Further Responses to Requests for Production of Documents, set one (“RPD”).  The Court is not in receipt of an opposition brief.  The Court notes that, pursuant to C.R.C. Rule 8.54(c), a failure to oppose a motion may be deemed consent to its being granted.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

A motion to compel further RPD responses may be brought based on: (1) incomplete statements of compliance; (2) inadequate, evasive, or incomplete claims of inability to comply; or (3) unmerited or overly generalized objections.  (C.C.P. § 2031.310(a).) 

 

A motion to compel further production must set forth specific facts showing good cause justifying the discovery sought by the inspection demand and be accompanied by a meet and confer declaration. (C.C.P. § 2031.310(b)(1).)  “Good cause” is shown by “a disputed fact that is of consequence in the action and the discovery sought will tend in reason to prove or disprove that fact or lead to other evidence that will tend to prove or disprove the fact.”  (Digital Music News LLC v Superior Court (2014) 226 Cal.App.4th 216, 224.)  The motion must be made within 45 days of service of the verified response or supplemental verified response, or on/before any specific late date to which the parties have agreed in writing.  (C.C.P. § 2031.310(c).) 

 

If the moving party has shown good cause for the requests for production, the burden is on the objecting party to justify the objections. (Kirkland v. Superior Court of Los Angeles County (2002) 95 Cal. App.4th 92, 98.) 

 

ANALYSIS:

 

Plaintiffs move to compel Defendant’s further responses to RPD Nos. 1-30. 

 

Plaintiffs propounded the RPDs on February 27, 2026 and Defendant responded with objections on April 15, 2026.  (Ardi Decl., ¶¶11-12, Ex. 1 [RPD], Ex. 2 [RPD Responses].)  On April 22, 2026, Plaintiffs’ counsel emailed defense counsel, requesting the documents promised in Defendant’s first set of responses and the parties agreed to meet and confer via telephone.  (Id., ¶15.)  On April 24, 2026, counsel conducted a meet-and-confer telephone call but were unable to reach an agreement on whether Defendant would provide supplemental responses.  (Id., ¶¶14, 16, Ex. 3.) 

 

Plaintiffs argue that the documents are relevant as they relate to Plaintiffs’ SBA claims; Plaintiffs’ own vehicle; Defendant’s warranty and replacement/repurchase policies, procedures, and practices; and Defendant’s knowledge of the same or similar defects in other vehicles of the same year, make, and model as the subject vehicle.  (Mot. at pp.6-9.) 

 

Defendant has not opposed the motion.  As noted above, Defendant’s failure to oppose the motion may be deemed as consent to its being granted.  Furthermore, it is Defendant’s burden, as the objecting party, to justify its objections, which it has failed to do.

 

As such, the motion to compel Defendant’s further responses to RPD Nos. 1-30 is granted.

 

Plaintiffs did not request sanctions.

 

--- 

 

RULING:

 

In the event a party requests a signed order or the court in its discretion elects to sign a formal order, the following form will be either electronically signed or signed in hard copy and entered into the court’s records. 

 

ORDER 

 

Plaintiffs Tereza Shahbazian and Emil Golanians’s Motion to Compel Further Responses came on regularly for hearing on July 31, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows:  

 

The Motion to Compel Defendant’s Further Responses to RPD, set one, NOS. 1-30 is granted.  Defendant is ordered to provide further responses within 30 days.

 

PLAINTIFF TEREZA SHAHBAZIAN TO GIVE NOTICE.

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.


Case Number: 25NNCV08943    Hearing Date: July 31, 2026    Dept: A

TENTATIVE RULING

JULY 31, 2026

DEMURRER WITH MOTION TO CONTINUE TRIAL

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 25NNCV08943

 

MP:     Defendant George C. Shen

RP:      Plaintiffs Yi-Xuan Shih and Chin Pang Lim  

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at [email protected] or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Yi-Xuan Shih aka Stacy Shih (“Shih”) and Chin Pang Lim (“Lim” (together, “Plaintiffs”) allege that Ying Chui Chen aka Jessica Chen (“Chen”), Chih Wei Li aka Raymond Li (“Li”), Henry Yee Szu (“Szu”), and George C Shen (“Shen”) (together, “Defendants”) engaged in a fraudulent scheme to extract money from Plaintiffs, who were vulnerable immigrants seeking lawful U.S. status.  Plaintiffs allege Defendants represented themselves as immigration professionals capable of obtaining EB-5 visas, work permits, and DACA approvals through connections with USCIS and the U.S. Military.  As a result of fabricated documents and misrepresentations, Plaintiffs contend they were induced to pay Defendants $43,000, which has not been returned. 

 

The First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), filed March 23, 2026, alleges: (1) Fraud (Intentional Misrepresentation); (2) Fraud (Concealment); (3) Breach of Contract; (4) Unjust Enrichment; (5) Conversion; (6) Civil Conspiracy; (7) Violation of Immigration Consultants Act (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 22440 et seq.); and (8) Violation of Unfair Competition Law (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 17200 et seq.).

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 22, 2026, Shen filed a “Demurrer of Defendant George C. Shen, to the First Amended Complaint of Plaintiffs Yi-Xuan Shih, aka Stacy Shih, and Chin Pang Lim; and a Motion to Continue Trial Date” [although no trial date has been set].  On April 30, 2026, Shih and Lim filed oppositions to the demurrer and the motion to continue.  On May 19, 2026, Shen filed a reply. 

 

Shen, Shih, and Lim are self-represented litigants. 

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

The grounds for a demurrer must appear on the face of the pleading or from judicially noticeable matters. (C.C.P. § 430.30(a); Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal. 3d 311, 318.) A demurrer for sufficiency tests whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Hahn v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.) The only issue involved in a demurrer hearing is whether the complaint states a cause of action. (Id.)

 

A demurrer assumes the truth of all factual, material allegations properly pled in the challenged pleading. (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at p. 318.) No matter how unlikely or improbable, the plaintiff’s allegations must be accepted as true for the purpose of ruling on the demurrer. (Del E. Webb Corp. v. Structural Materials Co. (1981) 123 Cal.  App. 3d 593, 604.) But this does not include contentions; deductions; conclusions of fact or law alleged in the complaint; facts impossible in law; or allegations contrary to facts of which a court may take judicial notice.  (Blank, supra, 39 Cal. 3d at 318.)

 

Pursuant to C.C.P. §§ 430.10(e) and (f), the party against whom a complaint has been filed may demur to the pleading on the grounds that the pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, or that the pleading is uncertain, ambiguous and/or unintelligible. It is an abuse of discretion to sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is a reasonable probability that the defect can be cured by amendment. (Schifando v. City of Los Angeles (2003) 31 Cal. 4th 1074, 1082.)

 

MEET AND CONFER:

 

C.C.P. §§ 430.41(a) and 435.5(a) require that the moving party meet and confer with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to the demurrer and/or motion to strike.

 

Shen did not accompany the demurrer with a meet and confer declaration.  Shih and Lim provide their joint declaration in opposition, stating that Shen did not meet and confer prior to filing the demurrer.  (Shih and Lim Decl., ¶¶2-3.) 

 

The Court has reviewed the email exchanges.  On April 10, 2026, Shen sent an email requesting that the parties meet and confer via telephone.  (Shih and Lim Decl., Ex. A.)  Plaintiffs declined a telephonic meet and confer arguing that the demurrer to the original complaint was moot in light of the FAC and that Shen’s email did not state the specific causes of action or basis for a demurrer to the FAC.  (Id., Ex. B.)  Shen responded that he was attempting to meet and confer regarding the FAC and his proposed demurrer to the FAC.  (Id., Ex. C.)  On April 17, 2026, Shen again emailed asking to meet and confer regarding the First to Eighth causes of action and requesting convenient times to conduct the meet and confer.  (Id., Ex. D.)  On April 20, 2026, Plaintiffs declined his request to meet and confer in person and informed Shen that they retained litigation counsel to handle the meet and confer process via video conference after he fulfilled his statutory obligations under C.C.P. § 430.41 to “identify with legal support the basis of the deficiencies.”  (Id. at Ex. E.)  Shen requested Plaintiffs’ counsel’s information to conduct meet and confer efforts.  (Id., Exs. F-H.)  On April 22, 2026, Plaintiffs again requested the legal support for Shen’s position and stated that after he sends this information, they will coordinate a time to schedule a video conference with their attorney. 

 

Shen made multiple attempts to meet and confer with Plaintiffs but was denied attempts to meet and confer telephonically and in person.  C.C.P. § 430.41(a) allows the demurring party (Shen) to meet and confer in person, by telephone, or by video conference and, as a part of the meet and confer process, he must identify all of the specific causes of action that he believes are subject to demurrer and identify with legal support the basis for the deficiencies.  There is no procedural hurdle in the statute requiring Shen to first provide the legal basis for his position before a meet and confer via video conference can be scheduled.  Rather, this section contemplates that the legal basis may be provided as the meet and confer conference is underway. 

 

Here, full meet and confer efforts were not achieved.  However, this does not appear to be Shen’s fault as Plaintiffs declined Shen’s requests to meet and confer and ignored Shen’s requests to disclose Plaintiffs’ counsel’s information.  (The Court notes that no substitution of attorney forms have been filed.)  Although Shen did not file a declaration, the email exchange provided in Plaintiffs’ opposition shows that Shen attempted to meet and confer but such efforts were declined by Plaintiffs.  (See C.C.P. § 430.41(a)(3)(B) [“The demurring party shall file and serve with the demurrer a declaration stating either of the following: … (B) That the party who filed the pleading subject to demurrer failed to respond to the meet and confer request of the demurring party or otherwise failed to meet and confer in good faith.”].)  As such, the Court will consider the merits of the demurrer.

 

DEMURRER ANALYSIS:

 

Shen demurs to each cause of action alleged in the FAC on the grounds that they fail to state sufficient facts and are uncertain. 

 

A.     First Cause of Action for Fraud (Intentional Misrepresentation) – Overruled

 

The elements for fraud are: (1) a representation, usually of fact, which is false; (2) knowledge of its falsity; (3) intent to defraud; (4) justifiable reliance upon the misrepresentation; and (5) damage resulting from that justifiable reliance.  (Stansfield v. Starkey (1990) 220 Cal. App. 3d 59, 72-73.)  This cause of action is a tort of deceit and the facts constituting each element must be alleged with particularity; the claim cannot be saved by referring to the policy favoring liberal construction of pleadings.  (Committee on Children's Television, Inc. v. General Foods Corp. (1983) 35 Cal.3d 197, 216.)  Since the claim must be pleaded with particularity, the cause of action based on misrepresentations must allege facts showing how, when, where, to whom, and by what means the misrepresentations were tendered.  (Stansfield v. Starkey (1990) 220 Cal.App.3d 59, 73.)

 

In the First Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants made numerous false representations of material facts to Plaintiffs that: (a) they were qualified and licensed to provide immigration services; (b) they had special influence and connections within USCIS; (c) Plaintiffs’ funds would be used for a legitimate EB-5 investment; (d) they had filed immigration applications on Plaintiffs’ behalf; and (e) Plaintiffs’ money could not be refunded because it had already been spent on legal and filing fees.  (FAC, ¶35.)  Plaintiffs allege that Chen and Li made various representations (id., ¶36(a)-(f), (h)-(i)) and that Shen represented through a falsified USPS mail receipt on July 17, 2024 that he had mailed an immigration application not USCIS (id., ¶36(g)).  Plaintiffs allege Defendants knew their representations were false because of Shen’s February 14, 2024 email circulating fabricated agreement templates, Defendants never intended to provide legitimate services, Szu’s admission the interviews were staged, and the fabricated USPS mail receipt.  (Id., ¶37.)  They claim the misrepresentations were made with the intent to induce Plaintiffs to pay money to Defendants, including the false representation about the DACA approval which induced Plaintiffs to make an additional $3,000 payment and prevent Plaintiffs from demanding a refund.  (Id., ¶38.)  They assert that they justifiably relied on Defendants’ misrepresentations because they appeared to be experts, fabricated credentials, had official-looking written agreements, met at a law office, staged government interviews, and falsified official documents.  (Id., ¶39.)  As a result, Plaintiffs were damaged in the amount of $43,000. (Id., ¶40.) 

 

In the FAC’s “Facts Specific to Each Defendant” section, Plaintiffs allege Shen was the self-styled “chief” of the operation and engaged in the following fraudulent acts: (1) on February 14, 2024, he sent an email to Li and Szu containing fraudulent investment agreements templates, which proves a premeditated conspiracy; (2) on April 24, 2024, Shen participated in a fabricated interview of Plaintiffs’ minor son when he met the son and Szu in the USCIS parking lot, took copies of passports, and left without conducting any legitimate proceeding to create the false appearance that the official process was underway; (3) on June 20, 2024, Shen was present the meeting when Li distributed fraudulent, unfiled immigration forms and he evasively claimed he did not know when Plaintiffs would receive their work permits; (4) on July 17, 2024, Shen provided Lim with a falsified USPS certified mail receipt regarding the USCIS application; and (5) on January 5, 2025, Shen sent an email to Plaintiff stating he needed to “withdraw” the DACA application but no application had been filed.  (FAC, ¶32.) 

 

Shen demurs to the First Cause of Action, arguing that the allegations refer to “Defendants” generally or refer to Chen and Li’s actions, but fail to allege specific facts against Shen.  

 

While the FAC refers to “Defendants” generally in some instances, the FAC, read as a whole, provides specific facts against Shen regarding what alleged misrepresentations he made and how he and Defendants engaged in acts amounting to fraud.  As alleged, the Court finds that Plaintiffs have alleged sufficient facts to support each element of Fraud against Shen.  As such, the demurrer to the First Cause of Action is overruled.

 

B.     Second Cause of Action for Fraud (Concealment) – Overruled

 

The elements for fraudulent concealment are: (1) the defendant must have concealed or suppressed a material fact; (2) the defendant must have been under a duty to disclose the fact to the plaintiff; (3) the defendant must have intentionally concealed or suppressed the fact with the intent to defraud the plaintiff; (4) the plaintiff must have been unaware of the fact and would not have acted as he did if he had known of the concealed or suppressed fact; and (5) as a result of the concealment or suppression of the fact, the plaintiff must have sustained damage.  (Lovejoy v. AT&T Corp. (2004) 119 Cal. App. 4th 151, 157-158.)

 

The duty to disclose arises where there is some relationship between the parties that give rise to a duty to disclose, such as a fiduciary, confidential, or a transactional relationship (seller/buyer, employer/prospective employee, doctor/patient, parties entering into a contractual agreement).  (Nissan Motor Acceptance Cases (2021) 63 Cal.App.5th 793, 826 [citations omitted].) For transactions without fiduciary or confidential relationships, “a cause of action for non-disclosure of material facts may arise in at least three instances: (1) the defendant makes representations but does not disclose facts which materially qualify the facts disclosed, or which render his disclosure likely to mislead; (2) the facts are known or accessible only to defendant, and defendant knows they are not known to or reasonably discoverable by the plaintiff; (3) the defendant actively conceals discovery from the plaintiff.”  (Id.)

 

In the Second Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants concealed/suppressed material facts, including that: (a) Defendants were not licensed attorneys, authorized immigration consultants, or registered immigration bond holders; (b) Defendants had no special influence with USCIS or any other government agency; (c) Defendants never intended to file any immigration applications on Plaintiffs’ behalf; (d) the “Brunswick Veterans Housing Services” entity named in the fraudulent agreement were fictitious or illegitimate; and (e) the USCIS “interviews” were staged.  (FAC, ¶44.)  Plaintiffs allege Defendants had a duty to disclose the material facts because they undertook to act as Plaintiffs’ immigration representatives, had exclusive knowledge of their lack of credentials and intent not to perform, and conducted staged interviews and falsified documents. (Id., ¶45.)  Plaintiffs claim Defendants intentionally concealed the facts to defraud Plaintiffs and prevent them from demanding a refund, such that Plaintiffs were unaware of the concealed facts and would not have paid $43000 had they known the truth.  (Id., ¶46.)  Plaintiffs allege that Shen held himself out as a high-ranking U.S. military officer and the “chief” of the operation, when he was not a licensed attorney, authorized immigration consultant, or a registered immigration bond holder.  (Id., ¶¶9, 45.)

 

Shen demurs to the Second Cause of Action, arguing that Plaintiffs did not identify what superior knowledge he had. He also argues that Plaintiffs refer to “Defendants” generally and fails to plead Fraud as to each defendant specifically.

 

The elements of fraudulent concealment do not necessarily require “superior knowledge” but rather that Defendants made representations but failed to disclose material facts that would render the facts misleading.  As framed by Plaintiffs, Defendants, including Shen, held themselves out to have credentials to perform immigration services on Plaintiffs’ behalf and while Defendants drafted documents, conducted interviews, and mailed documents, Plaintiffs alleged facts that these forms, interviews, and mailing were fabricated and that the immigration process was not progressing as represented.  Based on the transactional relationship the parties had (wherein Plaintiffs paid $43,000 in fees for services), the FAC sufficiently alleges Shen owed Plaintiffs a duty to disclose facts. 

 

The demurrer to the Second Cause of Action is overruled.

 

C.     Third Cause of Action for Breach of Contract – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

The elements for breach of contract are: “(1) the existence of the contract, (2) plaintiff's performance or excuse for nonperformance, (3) defendant's breach, and (4) the resulting damages to plaintiff.”  (Oasis West Realty, LLC v. Goldman (2011) 51 Cal.4th 811, 821.) 

 

In the Third Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege that the parties entered into a partially oral and written contract based on oral representations made on February 11 and 15 that was memorialized in the Agreement for Investment and Immigration and Private Contract for Investment and Immigration on February 15 and 16, 2024.  (FAC, ¶50, Exs. 13-14.)  Plaintiffs allege they performed under the agreements by paying $40,000 on February 16, 2024 and an additional $3,000 on April 2, 2024, as well as providing personal identifying information and their son attending the “interview.”  (Id., ¶51.)  Plaintiffs claim Defendants breached the agreement by failing to prepare and file any immigration applications, obtain immigration benefits, and provide legitimate immigration services.  (Id., ¶52.) 

 

According to the Immigration Investment Agreement, Shih was required to pay an initial $400,000 deposit to secure a position in the queue to start the USCIS application process, and the full amount of the investment was to be $800,000 with the remainder to be paid upon receiving the I-526 (temporary status) or within three months of initiating the visa application.  (FAC, Ex. 13 [Immigration Investment Agreement, ¶¶1.1, 1.5, 1.6].) According to the Investment Agreement, Shih was required to invest $800,000 in full and pay an additional $120,000 as a management fee (for attorney’s fees, regulatory application fee, and other service charges.)  (FAC, Ex. 14 [Investment Agreement at ¶1].) 

 

Shen argues that Plaintiffs acknowledged Shih texted Chen on February 21, 2024 stating she was unable to borrow additional funds, wished to stop the investment, and unsuccessfully requested a refund.  (FAC, ¶19.)  Thus, Shen argues that Plaintiffs engaged in an anticipatory breach of the contract.  (See Central Valley General Hospital v. Smith (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 501, 514 [“[A]n anticipatory breach of contract occurs when the contract is repudiated by the promisor before the promisor's performance under the contract is due.”].)

 

Based on the allegations, Plaintiffs have not alleged sufficient facts regarding the second element of performance or excuse for nonperformance.  Plaintiffs do not allege they performed their obligations in compliance with the agreements.  If relying on the terms of the attached agreements, then Shih was required to make a $400,000 initial deposit, pay the remaining $400,000 after receiving temporary status, and also pay $120,000 in management fees.  Plaintiffs allege that they paid $43,000 but not the $400,000 amount. 

 

In opposition, Plaintiffs argue that the contract was fraudulently induced in the first place such that Defendants cannot use Plaintiffs’ inability to perform a fraudulent agreement as a shield against liability.  However, by bringing this Breach of Contract Cause of Action, Plaintiffs are conceding, for the purposes of this alternate theory from the Fraud Cause of Action, that the parties entered into valid contracts. 

 

To the extent Plaintiffs contend they were excused from nonperformance due to Defendants’ alleged fraudulent conduct, this should be further explained.  As currently alleged, the parties entered the agreements on February 15 and 16, 2024 and, less than a week later on February 21, 2024, Plaintiffs represented that they wished to stop the investment due to lack of funds—not on the basis of fraudulent conduct.  Plaintiffs have not alleged facts that they were excused from nonperformance because they suspected fraudulent conduct; rather, their suspicions only arose months later when the immigration process was purportedly underway. 

 

Plaintiffs should clarify this cause of action upon amendment and allege facts, if possible supporting the second element.  The demurrer to the Third Cause of Action is sustained with leave to amend.

 

D.    Fourth Cause of Action for Unjust Enrichment – Sustained Without Leave to Amend

 

Under California law, unjust enrichment is not a cause of action.  (Melchior v. New Line Productions, Inc. (2003) 106 Cal. App. 4th 779, 794.)  Instead, it is the failure to make restitution under circumstances where it is equitable to do so.  (Id.)  Unjust enrichment is a general principle, underlying various legal doctrines and remedies, rather than a remedy itself.  (Id.)  It is synonymous with restitution.  (Id.)  This is the basis for the general rule in California, which finds that unjust enrichment is not a cause of action, but a claim for restitution.  (Hill v. Roll Int'l Corp. (2011) 195 Cal. App. 4th 1295, 1307.)

 

Shen demurs to the Fourth Cause of Action, arguing that this is not a recognized cause of action and, because a contract exists, Plaintiffs’ claim for unjust enrichment fails. 

 

The demurrer to the Fourth Cause of Action is sustained without leave to amend because there is no cause of action for unjust enrichment.

 

E.     Fifth Cause of Action for Conversion – Overruled  

 

The elements for conversion are: (1) the plaintiff’s ownership or right to possession of the property; (2) the defendant’s conversion by a wrongful act or disposition of property rights, interfering with plaintiff’s possession; and (3) damages. (Lee v. Hanley (2015) 61 Cal.4th 1225, 1240; PCO, Inc. v. Christensen, Miller, Fink, Jacobs, Glaser, Weil & Shapiro, LLP (2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 384, 395.)  “Money cannot be the subject of a cause of action for conversion unless there is a specific, identifiable sum involved, such as where an agent accepts a sum of money to be paid to another and fails to make the payment.”  (PCO, Inc. v. Christensen, Miller, Fink, Jacobs, Glaser, Weil & Shapiro, LLP (2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 384, 395.)  “A party need only allege it is entitled to immediate possession at the time of conversion.  [Citations.] However, a mere contractual right of payment, without more, will not suffice.”  (Farmers Ins. Exchange v. Zerin (1997) 53 Cal.App.4th 445, 452 [internal quotation marks and citations omitted].)

 

Plaintiffs allege that they were the owners and rightful possessors of specific identifiable sums they paid to Defendants: (a) $40,000 paid via the cashier’s check on February 16, 2024; and (b) the $3,000 Zelle transfer made on April 2, 2024.  (FAC, ¶61.)  Plaintiffs claim that Defendants wrongfully took possession of the funds by means of fraudulent misrepresentations without any intention to provide immigration services.  (Id., ¶62.) 

 

Shen demurs to this cause of action, arguing that Plaintiffs only alleged that a check was voluntarily issued in connection with the alleged agreement, which establishes that this is a contract dispute and not a conversion issue. 

 

At the pleading stage, the Court will allow this cause of action to remain as an alternative cause of action to the Breach of Contract Cause of Action.  In the event no valid contracts existed between the parties, Plaintiffs may have a claim for conversion.  The demurrer to the Fifth Cause of Action is overruled.

 

F.     Sixth Cause of Action for Civil Conspiracy – Sustained with Leave to Amend

 

Under California law, conspiracy is not a cause of action, but a legal doctrine that imposes liability on persons who, although not actually committing a tort themselves, share with the immediate tortfeasors a common plan or design in its perpetration.  (Wyatt v. Union Mortgage Co. (1979) 24 Cal.3d 773, 784.)  A claim for conspiracy must be based on a wrongful act and the claim must allege: (1) the formation and operation of the conspiracy; (2) the wrongful act or acts done pursuant thereto; and (3) the damage resulting.  (Unruh v. Truck Insurance Exchange (1972) 7 Cal. 3d 616, 631.) 

 

In making allegations of conspiracy, bare legal conclusions, inferences, generalities, presumptions, and conclusions are insufficient.  (State of California ex rel. Metz v. CCC Information Services, Inc. (2007) 149 Cal. App. 4th 402, 419 [finding that allegations that defendants conspired to conceal improper loss valuations was insufficient].)  There must be allegations that the purported conspirators had actual knowledge of the planned tort and had the intent to aid in the commission of the tort.  (Kidron v. Movie Acquisition Corp. (1995) 40 Cal.App.4th 1571, 1580.)

 

In the Sixth Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants formed a conspiracy to defraud Plaintiffs on February 14, 2025, when Shen emailed Li and Szu with fraudulent agreement templates to be used to defraud Plaintiffs.  (FAC, ¶67.)  Plaintiffs allege that Chen, Shen, Li, and Szu engaged in specific actions in furtherance of the conspiracy.  (Id., ¶68(a)-(d).)  Specifically, with respect to Shen, Plaintiffs allege Shen circulated fraudulent agreement templates, staged fake USCIS interviews, provided a falsified USPS mail receipt, falsely claimed to withdraw a non-existent DACA application.  (Id., ¶68(b).) 

 

While the allegations appear to be tied to the Fraud causes of action, Plaintiffs have not alleged facts supporting the formation of a conspiracy between Defendants or that the purported co-conspirator Defendants acted with actual knowledge and intended to aid in the commission of the Fraud together.  Though certain inferences can be made from the allegations that Defendants may have engaged in a civil conspiracy to defraud Plaintiffs, as stated above, inferences and presumptions are insufficient to allege conspiracy. 

 

The demurrer to the Sixth Cause of Action is sustained with leave to amend.

 

G.    Seventh Cause of Action for Violation of Immigration Consultants Act (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 22440 et seq.) – Overruled.

 

“It is unlawful for any person, for compensation, other than persons authorized to practice law or authorized by federal law to represent persons before the Board of Immigration Appeals or the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services, to engage in the business or act in the capacity of an immigration consultant within this state except as provided by this chapter.”  (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 22440.)  

 

A person engages in the business or acts in the capacity of an immigration consultant when that person gives nonlegal assistance or advice on an immigration matter, such as by: (1) completing a form provided by a federal or state agency but not advising a person as to their answers on those forms; (2) translating a person’s answers to questions posed in those forms; (3) securing for a person supporting documents, such as birth certificates, which may be necessary to complete those forms; (4) submitting completed forms on a person's behalf and at their request to the USCIS; and/or (5) making referrals to persons who could undertake legal representation activities for a person in an immigration matter.  (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 22441(a.) 

 

“Every person engaged in the business, or acting in the capacity of, an immigration consultant who enters into a contract or agreement with a client to provide services shall, prior to providing any services, provide the client with a written contract, the contents of which shall be prescribed by the Department of Consumer Affairs in regulations.”  (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 22442(a).) 

 

It is unlawful for any person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of an immigration consultant to make false or misleading statements to a client while providing services to that client or make any guarantee or promise to a client, unless the guarantee or promise is in writing and the immigration consultant has some basis in fact for making the guarantee or promise.  (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 22444(a), (b).)

 

“A person claiming to be aggrieved by a violation of this chapter by an immigration consultant may bring a civil action for injunctive relief or damages, or both. If the court finds that the defendant has violated a provision of this chapter, it shall award actual damages, plus an amount equal to treble the amount of actual damages or one thousand dollars ($1,000) per violation, whichever is greater. The court shall also grant a prevailing plaintiff reasonable attorneys' fees and costs.”  (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 22446.5(a).) 

 

In the Seventh Cause of Action, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants are immigration consultants, engaged in business and acted in the capacity of immigration consultants, and provided non-legal assistance in immigration matters by preparing and filing EB-5 visa and DACA applications for compensation.  (FAC, ¶73.)  Plaintiffs allege Defendants committed numerous violations, including making misrepresentations about their credentials, status of applications, and the nature of interviews (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 22444); failing to provide a written contract compliant with section 22442; demanding and receiving fees before completing services pursuant to section 22443.1; and representing that Defendants could obtain a specific result guaranteeing visas and DACA status (section 22444(b).  (FAC, ¶74.)  Plaintiffs seek injunctive relief and damages under section 22446.5.  (Id., ¶75.) 

 

Shen demurs to this cause of action, arguing that Plaintiffs’ own allegations negate their claim because they allege that Defendants did not prepare or file immigration applications, did not represent them in immigration proceedings, and did not provide immigration-related services. 

 

Based on the facts alleged, Plaintiffs have sufficiently alleged that Shen was an “immigration consultant” as contemplated under the Business & Professions Code because they allegedly engaged in the business to provide the services covered by the law.  While it is true that Plaintiffs have not alleged that Shen completed forms provided by a federal or state agency, he translated Plaintiffs’ answers in the forms, he secured supporting documents for Plaintiffs, submitted completed forms on Plaintiffs’ behalf (on the contrary, Plaintiffs allege no forms were submitted), and/or referred Plaintiffs to an immigration attorney nevertheless Shen it is sufficiently alleged agreed to provide those services.  Bus. & Pro. Code 22441(a) does not limit the services to those categories, but simply provides a list which includes but is not limited to those actions.  Bus & Prof. Code §22443.3

 

As Plaintiffs have alleged this foundational requirement, the demurrer to the Seventh Cause of Action is overruled.

 

H.    Eighth Cause of Action for Violation of Unfair Competition Law (Bus. & Prof. Code, § 17200 et seq.) – Overruled

 

The purpose of the Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”) is to protect both consumers and competitors by promoting fair competition in commercial markets for goods and services.  (Buller v. Sutter Health (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 981, 986.)  Section 17200 defines unfair competition to mean and include “any unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business act or practice and unfair, deceptive, untrue or misleading advertising and any act prohibited by [the false advertising law (§ 17500 et seq.)].”  (Id.)  Since section 17200 is written in the disjunctive, a business act or practice need only meet one of the three criteria, i.e., unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent, to be considered unfair competition under the UCL.  (Id.)   

 

In order to plead a claim under Business and Professions Code § 17200, there must be allegations demonstrating that the Defendants engaged in an unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business act or practice.  (Paulus v. Bob Lynch Ford, Inc. (2006) 139 Cal.App.4th 659, 676-77.)  Further, to plead this statutory claim, the pleadings must state with reasonable particularity the facts supporting the statutory elements of the violation.  (Khoury v. Maly's of California, Inc. (1993) 14 Cal.App.4th 612, 619.)

 

A violation of the unfair prong of section 17200 involves an examination of the impact of the business practice on its alleged victim balanced against the reasons, justifications and motives of the alleged wrongdoer.  (Searle v. Wyndham Int'l (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 1327, 1334.)  An unfair business practice occurs when it offends an established public policy or when the practice is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous or substantially injurious to consumers.  (Id.)  In general, the unfairness prong has been used to enjoin deceptive or sharp practices.  (Id.)  However, the unfairness prong does not give the Courts a general license to review the fairness of contracts.  (Id.)  Plaintiffs allege Defendants’ conduct was unfair, immoral, unethical, and unscrupulous such that Plaintiffs lost $43,000 and their personal identifying information has been exposed.  (FAC, ¶80.)  However, the allegations are conclusory.  A review of the pleadings reveals no allegations that identify a particular business practice that offends established public policy or that is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous, or substantially injurious to consumers. 

 

A violation of the unlawful prong includes anything that can properly be called a business practice and that at the same time is forbidden by law.  (Paulus v. Bob Lynch Ford, Inc. (2006) 139 Cal. App. 4th 659, 676-677.)  Plaintiffs allege that Defendants violated Business & Professions Code, § 22440 et seq., Penal Code, § 653.55 (“It is a misdemeanor for any person for compensation to knowingly make a false or misleading material statement or assertion of fact in the preparation of an immigration matter which statement or assertion is detrimentally relied upon by another.”), and Penal Code, § 484 (re theft).  (FAC, ¶79.)  For the reasons discussed above, Plaintiffs have not established the unlawful prong based on the Business & Professions Code.  Furthermore, Plaintiffs have not alleged, with specificity, the basis for their claim under the Penal Code.  At this time, a review of the pleadings reveals no allegations that identify a law, regulation, or statute and the particular business practices directed at Plaintiffs that violated the identified law, regulation, or statute. 

 

A violation of the fraudulent prong of section 17200 can be shown with allegations that the fraudulent practice was likely to deceive members of the public.  (Schnall v. Hertz Corp. (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1144, 1167.)  The “fraud” prong “is unlike common law fraud or deception. A violation can be shown even if no one was actually deceived, relied upon the fraudulent practice, or sustained any damage. Instead, it is only necessary to show that members of the public are likely to be deceived.”  (Buller v. Sutter Health (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 981, 986.)  Plaintiffs allege Defendants’ conduct was fraudulent in that it was likely to deceive the public, specifically vulnerable immigrants who lack knowledge of the U.S. immigration system, by fabricating credentials, official-looking documents, staged government proceedings, and falsified government receipts.  (FAC, ¶81.)  The Court finds that this allegation, in conjunction with the allegations above, are sufficient to satisfy the fraudulent prong. 

 

As one prong has been adequately alleged, the demurrer to the Eighth Cause of Action is overruled. 

 

MOTION TO CONTINUE TRIAL ANALYSIS:

 

Shen requests that the Court continue the trial date, arguing there is good cause since Shen cannot reasonably prepare for trial while the sufficiency of the pleadings remain unresolved.

 

There is no trial set in this action, and as such the motion is denied.  The only matter set after the July 31, 2026 hearing is a Case Management Conference scheduled for September 30, 2026.  As no trial has been set, the request for a trial continuance is denied as moot.

Case Number: 26NNCV01015    Hearing Date: July 31, 2026    Dept: A

MOTION TO QUASH SERVICE OF SUMMONS

Los Angeles Superior Court Case # 26NNCV01015

 

MP:     Defendant Walnut Creek 1 LLC

RP:      No opposition received    

 

NOTICE:

 

The Court is not requesting oral argument on this matter.  The Court is guided by California Rules of Court, Rule 3.1308(a)(1) whereby notice of intent to appear is requested.  Unless the Court directs argument in the Tentative Ruling, no argument is required and any party seeking argument should notify all other parties and the court by 4:00 p.m. on the court day before the hearing of the party’s intention to appear and argue.  The tentative ruling will become the ruling of the court if no argument is received.  

 

Notice may be given either by email at [email protected] or by telephone at (818) 260-8412.

 

ALLEGATIONS: 

 

Valentina Cevallos (“Plaintiff”) alleges that on December 8, 2025, she was walking across the shared yard at 3052 Burton Ave. in Rosemead when she was attacked by a pitbull which was kept on a long chain by tenant Defendant Angel Gonzalez (“Gonzalez”).  Plaintiff alleges that the dog lunged at her inner thigh and caused her to be thrown on the ground.  Plaintiff contends Defendant Walnut Creek 1 LLC (“Walnut”) and Gonzalez were previously notified that the pitbull posed a dangerous condition within the shared common area, but they failed to abate the hazard. 

 

The Complaint, filed February 11, 2026, alleges: (1) Premises Liability; and (2) General Negligence.

 

MOTION ON CALENDAR:

 

On April 24, 2026, Walnut filed a Motion to Quash Service of Summons and Complaint.  The Court is not in receipt of an opposition brief.  The Court notes that, pursuant to C.R.C. Rule 8.54(c), a failure to oppose a motion may be deemed consent to its being granted.

 

LEGAL STANDARD:

 

C.C.P. § 418.10(a)(1) states: “A defendant, on or before the last day of his or her time to plead or within any further time that the court may for good cause allow, may serve and file a notice of motion” to “quash service of summons on the ground of lack of jurisdiction of the court over him or her.”

 

C.C.P. § 415.20(b) states:  

 

(b) If a copy of the summons and complaint cannot with reasonable diligence be personally delivered to the person to be served, as specified in Section 416.60, 416.70, 416.80, or 416.90, a summons may be served by leaving a copy of the summons and complaint at the person's dwelling house, usual place of abode, usual place of business, or usual mailing address other than a United States Postal Service post office box, in the presence of a competent member of the household or a person apparently in charge of their office, place of business, or usual mailing address other than a United States Postal Service post office box, at least 18 years of age, who shall be informed of the contents thereof, and by thereafter mailing a copy of the summons and of the complaint by first-class mail, postage prepaid to the person to be served at the place where a copy of the summons and complaint were left. Service of a summons in this manner is deemed complete on the 10th day after the mailing.

 

(C.C.P. § 415.20(b).)

 

C.C.P. § 416.10 states in relevant part:

 

A summons may be served on a corporation by delivering a copy of the summons and the complaint by any of the following methods:

 

(a) To the person designated as agent for service of process as provided by any provision in Section 202, 1502, 2105, or 2107 of the Corporations Code (or Sections 3301 to 3303, inclusive, or Sections 6500 to 6504, inclusive, of the Corporations Code, as in effect on December 31, 1976, with respect to corporations to which they remain applicable).

 

(b) To the president, chief executive officer, or other head of the corporation, a vice president, a secretary or assistant secretary, a treasurer or assistant treasurer, a controller or chief financial officer, a general manager, or a person authorized by the corporation to receive service of process.

 

(C.C.P. § 416.10(a)-(b).) 

 

ANALYSIS: 

 

A.     Proof of Service

 

On March 12, 2026, Plaintiff filed the Proof of Service of Summons, indicating that Walnut had been served by substituted service on March 8, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. by serving “Park Grove – Agent for Service of Process.”  Registered process server, Homayon Taghavi, left the documents with “Rivas Mayela. Person in charge. (m/hisp/40/5’10/170/blk hair)” at the home located at 4758 Muscatel Avenue, Rosemead, CA 91770.  The documents were thereafter mailed on March 8, 2026. 

 

B.     Discussion

 

Walnut moves to quash service of the summons and complaint, arguing that Plaintiff has not established reasonable diligence before resorting to substituted service and service was not made on an authorized person. In California, a defendant's act of bringing a motion to quash service of a complaint under CCP § 418.10. does not establish that the defendant received valid statutory notice, nor does the defendant's actual notice of the lawsuit confer personal jurisdiction or cure defective service of process . Mannesmann Demag v. Superior Court (1985) 172 Cal. App. 3d 1118, 1124.  Under California law, while actual notice of the litigation is considered when determining whether a plaintiff has substantially complied with the service statutes, actual notice alone does not satisfy the statutory requirements for service of summons . Id., Dill v. Berquist Construction Co., 24 Cal. App. 4th 1426 (1994).

 

First, Plaintiff’s Proof of Service is not accompanied by a Declaration of Diligence showing that Plaintiff attempted to personally serve Walnut and/or the person apparently in charge.  “[A]n individual may be served by substitute service only after a good faith effort at personal service has first been made: the burden is on the plaintiff to show that the summons and complaint ‘cannot with reasonable diligence be personally delivered’ to the individual defendant. [Citations.] Two or three attempts to personally serve a defendant at a proper place ordinarily qualifies as ‘reasonable diligence.’ [Citation.]”  (American Express Centurion Bank v. Zara (2011) 199 Cal.App.4th 383, 389 [internal quotation marks and citations omitted].) 

 

Second, Walnut argues that Plaintiff did not serve an authorized person, a competent person “apparently in charge,” or a registered agent of Walnut.  Walnut argues that while Plaintiff served the documents at Walnut’s registered agent, Park Grove located at the Muscatel address, it argues that service was not effectuated on the proper designated agent or person authorized to accept service on Walnut’s behalf.  (See C.C.P. § 416.10.)

 

In support of the motion, Walnut provides its officer Van Nguyen’s declaration.  Mr. Nguyen states that there is no individual by the name of “Rivas Mayela” who was ever employed by Walnut or by its agent for service of process, and he has never heard of, met, or communicated with any individual with that name.  (Nguyen Decl., ¶¶3-4, 14.)  He states that at the time of the alleged service, he was Walnut’s only employee.  (Id., ¶¶4-6.)  (The Court notes that while Mr. Nguyen states he has attached Walnut’s employee list as Exhibit A, no exhibits accompany the motion or declaration papers.)  Mr. Nguyen states that Walnut does not employ any other individuals at the subject property or at the address associated with its agent for service of process, he was never served with the summons or complaint, and no competent person associated with Walnut was served as he is the only individual associated with Walnut’s business operations.  (Id., ¶¶8-10.)  He states that no officer, manager, member, employee, or authorized agent of Walnut was served with the summons and complaint.  (Id., ¶¶11-12.) He states if Walnut’s authorized individual or employee had been served, those documents would have been communicated to him or brought to Walnut’s attention, but this did not occur.  (Id., ¶13.)

 

Based on Mr. Nguyen’s declaration, Walnut has established that substituted service was not properly effectuated on Walnut’s designated agent for service of process or person apparently in charge.  Furthermore, the proof of service is not accompanied by a declaration of diligence detailing what efforts Plaintiff made prior to resorting to substituted service. 

 

The motion to quash is granted.

ORDER 

 

Defendant Walnut Creek 1 LLC’s Motion to Quash Service of Summons came on regularly for hearing on July 31, 2026, with appearances/submissions as noted in the minute order for said hearing, and the court, being fully advised in the premises, did then and there rule as follows:  

 

THE MOTION TO QUASH SERVICE OF THE SUMMONS AND COMPLAINT IS GRANTED.

 

THE CASE MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE SET FOR AUGUST 24, 2026 IS ADVANCED AND CONTINUED TO OCTOBER 28, 2026 AT 9:00 AM.
